 Good morning! Here's the latest in trending: 

 Nine years on: Tesla ( TSLA ) will deliver its Semi trucks to a first set of customers this week.

 Dashing hopes: No breakthroughs from Trump-Xi summit beyond the trade truce extension .

 Oil volatility:  Houthis attack more Saudi sites , while Hormuz reopening may be back in play .

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Top News
 
 
 
 Warning signal 
 
 
 
VisualAviation/iStock via Getty Images
 
 
Market anxiety over the AI infrastructure boom is on the rise, as the massive financing that backs this buildout is raising concerns over how risk is being allocated. Oracle ( ORCL ) sent a force majeure notice to the developer of a New Mexico  data center project in an effort to shield itself from rising expenses if the facility is delayed.

 What happened:  Oracle is reportedly trying to insulate itself from having to make payments if the 2.45 GW facility fails to come online in 2028 as was expected. The project already hit setbacks, including delays to a natural gas pipeline meant to feed the project. The data center, known as Project Jupiter, is being developed by Blue Owl Capital's ( OWL ) Stack Infrastructure. It is part of the broader Stargate Project involving Oracle, OpenAI ( OPENAI ) and SoftBank ( SFTBY ). About 20 banks provided an $18B loan to help finance the campus. Shares of Oracle, the facility's main tenant, and Bloom Energy ( BE ), whose fuel cells will power the project, fell over 3% on Thursday.  Project Jupiter "remains on our planned schedule," Oracle said, adding that it is confident in its path forward. Blue Owl  echoed the statement, saying the notice does not change the project's financial commitments.

 Dig deeper: The force majeure notice does not constitute an event of default on Oracle's financing deal. But even if the notice is intended as a precautionary step, it risks alarming lenders backing the project as the debt tied to it is already trading below 90 cents on the dollar. The update is "a logical follow-on to previously disclosed delays in powering the site," and by asserting force majeure now, Oracle "positions itself to defer payments on capacity it cannot yet energize," William Blair stated. "We would caution against an overreaction, as Bloom's 1.2 GW (up to 2.8 GW) master services agreement with Oracle expands across Oracle's portfolio and is not tied directly to one particular project," Evercore ISI pointed out. Bloom Energy could pivot capacity to other Oracle ( ORCL ) projects or other customers if necessary, Baird analyst Ben Kallo wrote.

 Credit risk:  Even so, Oracle's credit default swaps spiked to record highs on Thursday. The cost to insure the company's debt reached unprecedented levels, with the yield on its 6.7% bonds maturing in 2056 crossing 8% for the first time, according to Zerohedge. This yield noticeably exceeds the B2/B average of 7.5%. Currently holding a Baa2/BBB- rating, if downgraded to junk status, $120B of its bonds will be automatically removed from investment-grade indexes, Zerohedge warned. The credit squeeze extends beyond Oracle to other hyperscalers including Google ( GOOG ) ( GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Meta ( META ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ). Michael Burry, the famed "Big Short" investor, warned that Big Tech's huge AI infrastructure spending could eventually result in significant write-offs , "perhaps in 2028 or 2029."
